I am looking to subset the number of individuals contained in some populations in my genlight object where the number of individuals > 50 (in other populations in the gl, there are < 50 individuals, in which case I would retain all individuals). This is to check and account for the potential effect of unequal sample sizes on population clustering analyses.

Can you suggest the simplest way to do this subsetting within dartR, to subset some populations by number of individuals if the number of individuals > N, with the individuals to be retained/dropped within each population selected randomly? (of course selecting individs geographically within pops would be another game).

Thanks for your help,
Best wishes
Caroline.

messages.subject: Re: subset by number of individuals in a population?
messages.subject_clean: subset by number of individuals in a population?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Caroline,

Here is one way too do it.

Cheers,
Luis

library(dartR)
gl_test <- bandicoot.gl <http://bandicoot.gl>
# checking number of individuals per population
table(pop(gl_test))
# threshold of population size
pop_size_threshold <- 20
# separating populations
test <- seppop(gl_test)
# creating an empty element to merge back populations
out <- NULL
# using a for loop to sample individuals in each population
for (i in test){
  # if population has less individuals than the threshold, do nothing
  if (nInd(i)<=pop_size_threshold){
    # merge back populations
    out <- rbind(out,i)
    # if populations have more individuals than the threshold
  }else{
    # sampling at random individuals
    ind_sample <- sample(1:nInd(i),pop_size_threshold)
    # subsetting individuals
    tmp <- gl.keep.ind(i,ind.list = indNames(i)[ind_sample])
    #merging back populations
    out <- rbind(out,tmp)
  }
}

# checking number of individuals per population
table(pop(out))

messages.subject_clean: [dartR] subset by number of individuals in a population?
messages.body_plain:
As Renee has indicated, heterozygosity and comparison across studies and within studies is a difficult area.

(a) Comparing heterozygosity across populations of different species is measuring two components of difference -- one is the difference between the genomes in the proportion of sequence subject to SNP retention (e.g. neutral regions) and differences because of processes of population genetics. And then there are the different responses in the genetic contexts to the filtering needed to identify and score the SNPs. Probably best avoided except as broad-brush observations.
(b) If you are going to compare heterozygosity of subsets of your data (say for different populations), you need to be sure that the same SNP loci are represented in each subset, that is, do not filter out the monomorphs in each subset.
(c) Re-calling the SNPs for each subset will result in comparing chalk and cheese, best avoided, notwithstanding the approach presented in  https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/2041-210X.13659.
(d) Differential rates of missing values across subsets of your data will result in confounded comparisons. Filter heavily on missing values, and perhaps then use HWE imputation (gl.impute)
(e) Consider using gl.report.secondaries(), if you have enough data, to estimate the number of invariant sequence tags across your full dataset (post filtering), and use those to correct heterozygosity values.

They are my thoughts on the challenges. We need to work through this as a group and come up with some consistent dartR advice on heterozygosity supported by evidence.

Hope this helps.

A

messages.subject: Re: gl.read.dart() swapping 1 and 2 states?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The function gl.read.dart() reads reports provided by the sequencing company DArT. This company uses the format "0" = Reference allele homozygote, "1" = SNP allele homozygote, "2"= heterozygote. When the data is read by this function the format is changed.

In your case, you should use the function: gl.read.csv().

We have a detailed tutorial about how to read data that is not in DArT format:

http://georges.biomatix.org/storage/app/media/uploaded-files/tutorial3adartrdatastructuresandinput22-dec-21-2.pdf

Cheers,
Luis

library(poppr)

geni <- gl2gi(bandicoot.gl <http://bandicoot.gl>)
# Assign pop information to strata
strata(geni) <- data.frame(pop = pop(geni))
# Performing AMOVA
amova_poppr <- poppr.amova(geni,~pop,nperm = 100)

Cheers,
Luis

See https://www.journeybytes.com/fix-csv-sylk-error-in-excel/

Double check in a plain text editor that there isn't anything else
unexpected in the file and/or copy and paste it to a new text file and
save it, rename it as csv and see if that works.

I seem to recall having this problem once in the past.

Cheers
Peter

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] subset by number of individuals in a population?
messages.subject_clean: [dartR] subset by number of individuals in a population?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Arthur, Renee, Luis -

Thanks for your thoughtful responses and reminders of the non-triviality of this.

- Agreed - I have previously re-called SNPs to handle the individuals of two species separately in all subsequent filtering and analyses, but am not planning to make inferences from directly comparing heterozygosity across these data sets and different species.
- I’ll check again my rigour of filtering for missing values.
- I have been using gl.filter.secondaries to drop secondary SNPs across the data set.

Thanks for your support and also agreed - consistency of our approaches and standards as a group are important.

Best regards,
Caroline

> On 05 April 2022, at 08:08, Arthur Georges <ardy.g...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> As Renee has indicated, heterozygosity and comparison across studies and within studies is a difficult area.
>
> (a) Comparing heterozygosity across populations of different species is measuring two components of difference -- one is the difference between the genomes in the proportion of sequence subject to SNP retention (e.g. neutral regions) and differences because of processes of population genetics. And then there are the different responses in the genetic contexts to the filtering needed to identify and score the SNPs. Probably best avoided except as broad-brush observations.
> (b) If you are going to compare heterozygosity of subsets of your data (say for different populations), you need to be sure that the same SNP loci are represented in each subset, that is, do not filter out the monomorphs in each subset.
> (c) Re-calling the SNPs for each subset will result in comparing chalk and cheese, best avoided, notwithstanding the approach presented in  https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/2041-210X.13659.
> (d) Differential rates of missing values across subsets of your data will result in confounded comparisons. Filter heavily on missing values, and perhaps then use HWE imputation (gl.impute)
> (e) Consider using gl.report.secondaries(), if you have enough data, to estimate the number of invariant sequence tags across your full dataset (post filtering), and use those to correct heterozygosity values.
>
> They are my thoughts on the challenges. We need to work through this as a group and come up with some consistent dartR advice on heterozygosity supported by evidence.
>
> Hope this helps.
>
> A
>
> On Monday, April 4, 2022 at 3:54:50 PM UTC+10 renee....@gmail.com <http://gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Caroline,
> >
> > It’s worth keeping in mind that removing individual without re-calling SNPs may affect your results, depending on what questions you are asking. See: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/2041-210X.13659
> >
> > Sometimes subsetting individuals without re-calling your SNPs will be inappropriate to the question.
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> > Renee
> >
> > > On 4 Apr 2022, at 11:17 am, Jose Luis Mijangos <luis.m...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > Hi Caroline,
> > >
> > > Here is one way too do it.
> > >
> > > Cheers,
> > > Luis
> > >
> > > library(dartR)
> > > gl_test <- bandicoot.gl <http://bandicoot.gl/>
> > > # checking number of individuals per population
> > > table(pop(gl_test))
> > > # threshold of population size
> > > pop_size_threshold <- 20
> > > # separating populations
> > > test <- seppop(gl_test)
> > > # creating an empty element to merge back populations
> > > out <- NULL
> > > # using a for loop to sample individuals in each population
> > > for (i in test){
> > >   # if population has less individuals than the threshold, do nothing
> > >   if (nInd(i)<=pop_size_threshold){
> > >     # merge back populations
> > >     out <- rbind(out,i)
> > >     # if populations have more individuals than the threshold
> > >   }else{
> > >     # sampling at random individuals
> > >     ind_sample <- sample(1:nInd(i),pop_size_threshold)
> > >     # subsetting individuals
> > >     tmp <- gl.keep.ind(i,ind.list = indNames(i)[ind_sample])
> > >     #merging back populations
> > >     out <- rbind(out,tmp)
> > >   }
> > > }
> > >
> > > # checking number of individuals per population
> > > table(pop(out))

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
I was just wondering whether when DArT pre-filters the SNPs data before providing it to the final user, do they also remove potential PCR duplicates (that is "read duplicates", sequence reads that result from sequencing two or more copies of the exact same DNA fragment, and which are due to the fact that by mistake more than 1 PCR copy of the original DNA fragment hybridizes to the flow cell)?

As far as I understand, the "Clone ID" (which also matches the "Allele ID?) identifies unique target sequences (sequence tags), so that multiple sequence tags with the same Clone ID would represent "PCR duplicates", is that correct?

Does DArT already pre-filter and remove these PCR duplicates before providing the user with the final SNPs dataset, or should we filter PCR duplicates ourselves?
And if we have to filter out "PCR duplicates" ourselves, is the "gl.filter.cloneid" function the correct one to use?

When I try to use "gl.filter.cloneid", no loci are filtered out...I assume that is also because I had already filtered out secondaries with "gl.filter.secondaries".
In the DArTR manual, it says:
"gl.filter.secondaries: SNP datasets generated by DArT include fragments with more than one SNP and record them separately with the same CloneID (=AlleleID). These multiple SNP loci within a fragment (secondaries) are likely to be linked, and so you may wish to remove secondaries"

Would the "gl.filter.secondaries" function also have removed potential PCR duplicates?

I would really appreciate your help on this matter.
Thank you.
Best,
Gabriella

messages.subject: Re: "PCR duplicates" & "Clone ID"/gl.filter.cloneid?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabrielle,

The occurrence and management of multiple SNPs scored from a single sequence tag is a different issue from PCR duplicates. As I understand it, PCR duplicates result from sequencing two or more copies of the same fragment of DNA. Setting aside the possibility of sequencing errors, PCR duplicates can make the occurrence of the affected allele appear proportionately more abundant than it should compared to the other allele. This could potentially have an effect on the calls, particularly for heterozygotes. Most workflows have ways of detecting and eliminating PCR duplicates.

As for how DArT does this, that is a question for DArT not dartR. dartR only deals with post-processing after DArT has weaved its magic. dartR works from the DArT reports and does not delve down into the pipelines used by DArT to deliver reliable SNP and SilicoDArT data.

So you need to address this question to Diversity Arrays Technology.

Multiple SNPs scored from a single sequence tag -- we do manage those in dartR because they are included in the DArT reports. The relevant scripts are gl.report.secondaries and gl.filter.secondaries as you have indicated.

All the best, and hope you had a happy Easter break.

Arthur

messages.body_plain:
HI,

The patterns in your PCoA/Structure plots might indicate many things including that these individuals could be a different species or migrants from a distant population.

To identify a specific individual in a PCoA plot, you could use the interactive option as shown below:

> pcoa <- gl.pcoa(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>)
> gl.pcoa.plot(pcoa,platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>,interactive=TRUE)

Other functions that could help you to visualise overall patterns are:
- matrix of the probability of identity by descent:
> gl.grm(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>, legendx = 0.05, legendy = 0.5)
- genotypes by individual and population:
> gl.smearplot(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>,ind_labels = TRUE, group_pop = TRUE)

Other analyses that you could perform that could give you more information"
- gl.nhybrids()
- gl.report.pa <http://gl.report.pa>()
- gl.fixed.diff()

Cheers,
Luis

messages.subject: Re: Identify clonal genotypes from a dataset
messages.subject_clean: Identify clonal genotypes from a dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

We don't have a function specifically for identifying clones, but you can use the function to calculate the proportion of shared alleles between individuals: gl.propShared().
If you have clones in your dataset, pairs of individuals should have a very high value, say more than 99%.

Here is some example code for this approach.

library(dartR)
# calculating the proportion of shared alleles
res <- gl.propShared(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl/>)
# converting a matrix into columns
clones_temp <- as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(res)))
# filtering individuals using a threshold of 0.99
clones_temp_2 <- clones_temp[clones_temp$Freq>0.99,]
# getting pairs of individuals that are not the same
clones <- clones_temp_2[which(clones_temp_2$Var1!=clones_temp_2$Var2),]

To have more security in the results, I would recommend that you eliminate the loci that have missing data using a very conservative threshold, for example: gl.filter.callrate(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>,threshold = 1)

Cheers,
Luis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

Not sure if that helps. Below is a script I developed with a colleague looking in the reproduction modes in ferns.

The genlight object (fern.catch) has populations and I compare within each population the individuals and there genotypes.

The output is the number of mismatches for clones, selfing and parent-offsprings between pairs of individuals in a population.

So you should get the clones by looking at the mismatches in the clonemm column (there might be a few due to genotyping errors so you need to define a threshold, when you call a clone).

The other mismatches indentify selfing and parent-offspring relationship, but are naturally less precise (we do not know the parents).

The output is a list that has a data.frame for  each population. So if you do not have population simply define a single population for your genlight object.

Hope that helps,

Cheers, Bernd

#compare within catchments

pops <- seppop(fern.catch)

#check mismatches

res <- list()

for (ii in 1:length(pops))

{

pp <- pops[[ii]]

m <- as.matrix(pp)

#allpairs

cb <- t(combn(nInd(pp),2))

df <- data.frame(nind1=cb[,1], nind2=cb[,2], ind1=indNames(pp)[cb[,1]], ind2=indNames(pp)[cb[,2]], nloc=NA, clonemm =NA, selfmm=NA, pomm=NA, clonemmp=NA, selfmmp=NA, pommp=NA)

nl <- nLoc(pp)

for (i in 1:nrow(df))

{

                i1 <- m[df$nind1[i], ]

                i2 <- m[df$nind2[i], ]

                miss <- is.na <http://is.na>(i1) | is.na <http://is.na>(i2)

                i1c <- i1[!miss]

                i2c <- i2[!miss]

                ncom <- nl-sum(miss)

                #cloning mismatches

                cmm <- sum(i1c!=i2c)

                #selfing missmatches

                smm <- sum(i1c==0 & i2c!=0) + sum(i1c==2 & i2c!=2)

                #po missmatches

  pomm <- sum(i1c==0 & i2c==2)+ sum(i1c==2 & i2c==0)

                df[i,5:11]<- c(ncom, cmm, smm, pomm, cmm/ncom, smm/ncom, pomm/ncom)

}

res[[ii]] <- df

}

names(res)<- names(pops)

messages.subject: Re: Equation for PIC
messages.body_plain:
Hello Francine,

This is the code used to calculate PIC.

I hope it is what you are looking for.

Cheers,
Luis

# converting genlight object to matrix
t <- as.matrix(x)
# number of homozygotes for the reference allele
c0 <- colSums(t == 0, na.rm = T)
# number of heterozygotes
c1 <- colSums(t == 1, na.rm = T)
# number of homozygotes for the alternative allele
c2 <- colSums(t == 2, na.rm = T)
# total number of genotypes
c <- (c0 + c1 + c2)
OneRatioRef <- (c0 + c1) / c
OneRatioSnp <- (c1 + c2) / c
ZeroRatioRef <- 1 - OneRatioRef
ZeroRatioSnp <- 1 - OneRatioSnp
PICRef <- 1 - ((OneRatioRef * OneRatioRef) + (ZeroRatioRef * ZeroRatioRef))
PICSnp <-  1 - ((OneRatioSnp * OneRatioSnp) + (ZeroRatioSnp * ZeroRatioSnp))
AvgPIC <- (PICRef + PICSnp) / 2

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Percentage contribution PCA
messages.body_plain:
The absolute value of percentage explained on an axis is not a good indication of whether or not that axis has captured substantial structure. The value needs to be taken in the context of the other eigenvalues. Is it substantially greater than the average percentage explained by all the PCA axes (Guttman criterion)? Or, because the “noise” eigenvalues can be expected to decline geometrically, you can log them and see if the eigenvalue for PCA 1 is greater than expected on consideration of the confidence limits for the prediction of y against x.

Lots of ways to skin this cat. But if you are working with 10000 axes, then 1% could be quite substantial if not spectacularly convincing.

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Combining datasets
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

As Olly said, it is not advisable to merge two datasets with a different number of loci and different individuals, so the reanalysis of the two datasets from DArT is the safest option. This issue has been discussed previously in the forum, see:

https://groups.google.com/g/dartr/c/ay0TJ00hRPc/m/Um2Uy56ABwAJ

Having said that, please find below some code of how to do the merging. This would work assuming that DArT assigned the same loci names to all the jobs of the same species. I asked DArT bioinformaticians about loci names in different jobs from the same species, they said:

"The SNP names which contain ID numbers less than 100,000,000 would be the same between reports in general, however, in it also depends on whether or not the 2 species have been assayed under the same organism designation.
I would definitely recommend to request a co-analysis rather than try to combine the results."

Another potential source of bias would be that the reference allele is used in the names of the loci. The reference allele is based on the allele with higher frequency. This means that the reference allele could be different in different populations.

If you have a reference genome, one possible solution would be to map the trimmed sequences in both datasets using the function gl.blast.

Cheers,
Luis

library(dartR)
# test dataset
df_test <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl/>
df_test <- gl.filter.callrate(df_test,threshold = 1)
df_test <- gl.filter.monomorphs(df_test)
#test dataset 1
test <- gl.keep.ind(df_test,ind.list = indNames(df_test)[1:5])
test <- gl.keep.loc(test, loc.list = locNames(test)[1:6])
#test dataset 2
test_2 <- gl.keep.ind(df_test,ind.list = indNames(df_test)[6:10])
test_2 <- gl.keep.loc(test_2, loc.list = locNames(test_2)[6:11])
# finding loci in common
common_loc_test <- locNames(test)[locNames(test) %in% locNames(test_2)]
common_loc_test_2 <- locNames(test_2)[locNames(test_2) %in% locNames(test)]
# keeping only loci in common
test <- gl.keep.loc(test,loc.list = common_loc_test)
